pages.text: On August 5, 2024, many people in Dhaka, Bangladesh, protested. They wanted the government to change. The government had been in power for 15 years. After the protests, the prime minister left the country. People were happy because they wanted more accountability. The protests started because of rules about government jobs. Then, the movement grew.

pages.text: Sadly, about 1,400 people died during this time. The government fell, but people wanted more than just a new government. They wanted better laws and stronger institutions. Now, two years later, people are asking questions. Did the system really change? Some student leaders say that the big changes they wanted did not happen.

People expected reforms in the courts and other state offices. However, some old ways of working are still there. Some experts say that holding an election is a good first step for democracy. But they also say that keeping democracy strong is hard work. It takes a long time to build a fair system.
People are still waiting to see if the promises from the protests will become real in the future.

pages.text: The human cost was significant, with the OHCHR reporting approximately 1,400 deaths during the unrest. Following the resignation and departure of the prime minister, the nation celebrated a clear victory, yet the long-term impact remains a subject of intense debate. Two years later, the focus has shifted from the fall of a regime to the stability of the new system.

While an election has since taken place, providing a democratic signal, many citizens and activists argue that the structural changes they demanded have not materialized. Student leader Hasnat Abdullah noted that the fundamental institutions—including the judiciary and executive branches—have not undergone the deep reforms many expected.

Instead, critics observe that old political habits and structures persist, leading to a decline in public optimism. Data from the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development shows that public confidence in the country's direction dropped from 71 percent in August 2024 to 42 percent by July 2025.

While the government describes its legislative actions as a necessary review process, opposition groups express concern over the slow pace of reform. Ultimately, the question remains whether the July uprising succeeded in merely changing the faces in power or if it truly established the checks and balances necessary for a functioning democracy.

pages.text: The events of August 5, 2024, in Dhaka, Bangladesh, marked a watershed moment in the nation's political history. Following 15 years of entrenched rule, the government collapsed under the weight of mass protests fueled by grievances over authoritarianism and a lack of institutional accountability.

pages.text: The uprising, which originated as a localized movement for quota reform, rapidly evolved into a broader societal demand for systemic overhaul. The human toll was profound, with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights documenting approximately 1,400 fatalities between July 1 and August 15, 2024.

The subsequent resignation of Sheikh Hasina provided a visible, immediate outcome, yet the transition has since faced complex challenges regarding the depth of state reform. In the two years following the uprising, the discourse has transitioned from the euphoria of regime change to a critical assessment of democratic consolidation.

While the return to electoral processes has been cited by some observers as a sign of progress, others, including key student leaders like Hasnat Abdullah, contend that the structural transformations promised during the protests remain largely unfulfilled.

There is a palpable tension between the government's characterization of its legislative reviews as necessary amendments and the concerns of activists who perceive a regression toward old political habits. This skepticism is reflected in longitudinal surveys; the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development reported a decline in public optimism, with positive sentiment regarding the country's trajectory falling from 71 percent in August 2024 to 42 percent by July 2025.

The core challenge lies in the distinction between the removal of political power and the reconstruction of state institutions. Critics point to the persistence of controversial practices, such as the renaming of security units and the slow pace of judicial and constitutional reform, as evidence that the underlying machinery of the state remains largely unchanged.

As the nation navigates this period of uncertainty, the ultimate test of the July uprising will not be the change in leadership, but the extent to which the promised checks and balances, civil rights, and institutional accountability are embedded into the fabric of the state. Whether these democratic aspirations take root remains an open, unresolved question.

pages.text: Brasília is a city in Brazil. It was built to be a green city with many trees. But some areas are very different. In the Sol Nascente favela, there is a lot of concrete and very few trees. It is much hotter there than in the center of the city.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Reflection of Parque Cultural Paulista building in Avenida Paulista, Brazil

pages.text: The heat is a big problem for people living in Sol Nascente. Francisco Silva is a resident there. He says the air does not move and it is very dry. This makes it hard for him to breathe. He tries to stay cool by using wet towels and planting trees near his home.

Experts say that poor areas often have less green space. This is called an urban heat island. Some people are now planting gardens to help. One woman, Nasaré Francisca da Silva, turned a place full of trash into a small forest. Now, people can go there to stay cool. The government wants to plant more trees in the future.
They hope this will help people stay healthy when it gets very hot.

evidence: Brasília was designed to be a green city.
Sol Nascente consists of mostly tarmac-surfaced streets, with houses crammed on top of one another and narrow pavements that can barely accommodate pedestrians, let alone trees.
Nasaré Francisca da Silva waters crops at Floresta da Nasaré, in Ceilândia, Brazil, where her agroforestry project emerged from a rubbish tip.

pages.text: Brasília was originally planned as a green city, featuring tree-lined avenues and parks. However, this vision is not shared by all its residents. In the Sol Nascente favela, located 30 kilometers from the city center, the landscape is dominated by concrete and tarmac.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Reflection of Parque Cultural Paulista building in Avenida Paulista, Brazil

pages.text: A study by the University of Brasília highlights that some peripheral areas have up to 23 times less green space than the central Plano Piloto. The lack of vegetation creates an urban heat island effect, where temperatures in Sol Nascente can reach 46.6ºC. Residents like Francisco Silva report severe health issues, including respiratory problems caused by dry air and dust.

To cope, Silva has started planting trees and modifying his home to improve airflow. Experts note that this disparity in green space access is a global issue, often linked to socio-economic status. While the government has announced plans to address this green deficit, progress is slow due to infrastructure challenges like narrow pavements.

In the meantime, community-led initiatives are making a difference. Nasaré Francisca da Silva, for instance, transformed a former rubbish tip into a thriving agroforestry project. Her work provides a cooling sanctuary for neighbors and serves as a model for grassroots environmental action in the face of rising temperatures.

pages.text: Mob violence is a big problem in Bangladesh. A group called ASK says that 154 people died from mob attacks between January and August 2026. People often take the law into their own hands. They attacked him, but other reporters saved him. Another journalist, Jamal Ruhany, says people often attack others without knowing if they are guilty. The government says it will stop this violence. They want to use more police and cameras. However, many people still worry about safety and justice.

attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation

pages.text: Justino is a journalist from Myanmar. He wanted to be a reporter since he was 10 years old. He wanted to help people by sharing their stories. He started his work after the 2021 coup. Being a journalist is very hard. Justino saw many bad things. He felt a lot of stress and fear.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Old Bagan, Myanmar, Landscape of ancient Bagan city

pages.text: In October 2025, he wrote about a group in the Magway Region. The group was not happy. They put his name on the internet. He received many threats. He had to move to many different places to stay safe. He also wrote about gold mining and other problems. It was dangerous work.

In 2026, someone said they wanted to hurt him. He had to leave his home. Now, he lives in a border area. He is still afraid, but he wants to keep working. He says that telling the truth is important. He is learning to be strong and take care of his mental health. He believes his work helps people.

evidence: Ever since I was around 10 years old — old enough to begin thinking seriously about the world — I admired journalists.
Exile Hub is one of Global Voices’ partners in Southeast Asia, emerging in response to the 2021 coup in Myanmar, and focusing on empowering journalists and human rights defenders.
One experience that remains deeply etched in my memory took place in October 2025.

pages.text: Justino, a journalist from Myanmar, shares his challenging journey in a recent article published on August 12, 2026. Since childhood, he dreamed of bringing people's voices to light. However, after the 2021 coup, he discovered that the reality of reporting on the ground was far more demanding than he had imagined.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Old Bagan, Myanmar, Landscape of ancient Bagan city

pages.text: His work often involves investigating human rights violations, which has taken a significant toll on his mental health. In October 2025, while investigating a case in the Magway Region, he faced severe backlash from a local resistance group. After he reported on their actions, his personal information was leaked, leading to online threats and increased surveillance by military authorities.

He was forced to move constantly to avoid arrest. The situation worsened in 2026 when he faced direct threats to his life, forcing him to flee to a border area. Despite the constant fear and psychological trauma, Justino remains committed to his profession.

He emphasizes the importance of self-care and resilience, noting that no story is worth more than a journalist's life. He continues to work, driven by the belief that his reporting serves the public interest and brings necessary truth to light.
